item.title: The Price of Flexibility
item.description:
Anxiety

The Price of Flexibility

Why remote work deepens the mental health crisis, and how to fix it.

Posted July 2, 2026

Key points
  • Human beings aren't meant to operate entirely in a digital vacuum.
  • A jaw-dropping 84 percent of remote employees spend their entire working day completely alone.
  • Employees in work-from-home roles have experienced more spikes in distress and mental health visits.
  • We have to reshape the very blueprint of how we work and how we interact with fellow humans.

Today, roughly 35 million Americans log into work without ever leaving their houses. At first glance, the setup looks like an absolute dream come true. The perks seem completely undeniable: You get to delete exhausting daily commutes from your life, permanently evade overbearing bosses, and wave goodbye to a massive chunk of workplace headaches. It sounds like the ultimate professional cheat code—total freedom, zero corporate noise, and absolute comfort.

Yet, when you look past the cozy sweatpants and the lack of a morning rush hour, a much darker picture begins to emerge. Shocking data tracking more than half a million Americans over the last 15 years has pulled back the curtain on a painful, inescapable reality. As it turns out, despite the seductive flexibility and autonomy it promises, remote work has actually acted as an accelerant for a quiet epidemic, dramatically driving up feelings of deep isolation and severe psychological distress across the workforce.

In fact, alarming research highlighted in The New York Times suggests that the massive societal shift toward working from home is responsible for a staggering one-third of the entire decline in American mental health observed between 2011 and 2024. Now, this data isn't trying to argue that meaningful, high-level productivity can happen only when you are chained to a desk in a traditional, fluorescent-lit office building. However, it serves as a massive wake-up call. It proves that human beings simply aren't meant to operate entirely in a digital vacuum, and it means that both forward-thinking companies and everyday employees must start aggressively prioritizing real, unfiltered, face-to-face connection before the social fabric of our working world unravels completely.

When you dig into the data, the numbers paint a staggeringly bleak picture of just how isolating the virtual office truly is. A jaw-dropping 84 percent of remote employees spend their entire working day completely, utterly alone, while more than half report feeling a profound and distinct lack of connection to the people they work with. We tell ourselves that Slack, Zoom, and Teams bridge the gap, but they don't. Even with constant, 24/7 access to digital communication apps, work-from-home employees receive significantly less professional feedback and interact with fewer people outside their tight, immediate bubbles.

You might assume that these workers compensate for a lonely 9-to-5 by aggressively socializing once the laptop closes, but the reality is exactly the opposite. Surprisingly, they don't make up for the deficit at all. Instead, days may blur together and pass without a single shred of real-world human contact.

This absence of daily friction feeds directly into a psychological "use it or lose it" cycle. A comfortable but dangerous rut becomes established, and over time, the once-effortless act of reaching out, making plans, and actually spending time with other human beings begins to feel incredibly difficult, peculiar, and deeply awkward. And as for meeting brand-new people? You can completely forget about that, too.

Behind the Distress—And the Blueprint for a Fix

With routine, everyday social encounters suddenly wiped off the calendar, employees in work-from-home roles have experienced unprecedented spikes in psychological distress, clinical mental health visits, and prescriptions for psychotropic medications compared to their on-site peers. This isn't a temporary funk, either. This steep rise in depression started back in 2020 and has stubbornly refused to ease up, pointing directly to remote work as a major catalyst.

To make matters worse, this shift didn't happen exclusively. It collided perfectly with the rise of hyper-addictive social media platforms and the excessive screen time that dominates our modern lives—a highly solitary, passive activity that only exacerbates the sense of baseline loneliness.

As economists Emma Harrington and Natalia Emanuel pointed out in The New York Times: "Our brains are wired to connect face-to-face, and even the most advanced digital tools are a poor substitute. To maintain this critical source of connection, workers need doses of in-person time with one another." Even so, the answer to this crisis isn't as simple as launching a corporate mandate to force everyone back into cubicles and rewinding the clock to 2019. We can't forget that the old pre-pandemic grind—where people were expected to spend every single waking hour chained to an office desk—was seriously flawed, often negating precious time for friends, family, and personal well-being.

A Shared Responsibility for Connection: Reimagining How We Bond at Work

At the end of the day, curing the isolation epidemic isn't a one-way street; building a meaningful, connected workplace culture requires a coordinated effort from both sides of the desk. On an individual level, everyday employees can take charge of their own social health by stepping up to the plate—whether that means inviting a nearby colleague out for lunch, planning casual coffee dates, or organizing fun group activities, as Harrington and Emanual suggest.

They also emphasize that companies must actively step in to bridge the gap and make face-to-face connection seamless. The good news? Forward-thinking employers are already getting creative. Instead of relying on awkward corporate icebreakers, they are restructuring annual performance reviews to explicitly acknowledge and reward the crucial, yet historically invisible, emotional labor of building team cohesion.

Other organizations are completely blowing up traditional office layouts. They are building centralized in-office communal hubs designed specifically to force people out of their bubbles and spark serendipitous, casual interactions. Some companies are establishing weekly one-on-one and group sessions where coworkers from different departments can get together to unpack recent wins and vent about shared frustrations.

Ultimately, these strategic, human-centric workplace interventions do far more than just foster a warm sense of community and sharpen collaboration skills. If we want to ensure that work remains a genuine, life-giving source of human connection, we have to change much more than just the physical coordinates of our desks. We have to reshape the very blueprint of how we work and how we interact with fellow humans.

item.title: Structure That Sustains but Then Constrains Must Be Broken
item.description:
Growth Mindset

Structure That Sustains but Then Constrains Must Be Broken

Growth sometimes requires abandoning structure that no longer helps.

Posted July 2, 2026

Key points
  • Structure can provide comfort, safety, and capacity.
  • Structure that stays rigidly constant and independent of function can interfere with and prevent growth.
  • Breaking structure is eventually required in order to develop enhanced function and capacity.

When we create or build something, we often need temporary supports to help guide us and keep things in place. Sometimes those temporary structures become embedded within whatever we are building and just stay there in a support capacity, possibly forever. Sometimes those supports that at one time helped us set something up subsequently prevent us from growing.

It's not a shoo-in

There's a concept in traditional Japanese martial arts that explains the stages of development and maturation with ongoing training: shu ('shoo') ha ('hah') ri ('ree').

Shu 守 is often functionally translated along the lines of "conserve/protect/follow." This implies that in the early stages of training, we need to follow a model and use that semi-rigid structure to help support our development. Adherence to a set mold is a key idea to help guide our training.

Ha 破 usually means to move away from, detach, or break away. This implies that we are at a stage of understanding where a rigid structure is no longer necessary to support our training. We can begin to break the mold and move away from the rigidity of the prior structure.

Ri 離 has a meaning of transcendence or departure. At this very late stage of training, we no longer need any of the supporting structure of the mold to continue our development. We are independent of past constraints and are free to develop. Contents within the prior structures may still be used but have a very different context and meaning.

The point of all of this is that change is required for continual development. In a martial arts context, this means a very fluid approach to just about everything, bringing to mind Bruce Lee's advice to "be like water." This concept is found in every martial art to a certain extent, but especially emphasized in traditions like Bagua Zhang and Wing Chun Kuen. There is an explicit focus on the development of structure and then freeing ourselves of the structure to live in the moment during our responses.

Staying the same requires changes

In a martial arts context as well as broader life activities, we are striving for development, improvement, and maturation. Do you want to master a strategy or do you want to master yourself? Or, as I often discuss with martial arts trainees, are you trying to master a martial art or become a master of martial arts? These are related but not the same pursuits.

In some ways, this is like that famous quote, "For everything to stay the same, everything must change," found in the 1958 novel The Leopard by Giuseppe Tomasi di Lampedusa. In this case, the thing we want to stay the same is our continued development—we want to maintain a growth mindset—whereas everything that supports growth must change and expand to allow it.

Black belt brain injury

In the early stages of my journey back from brain injury, I relied a lot on rigid structures for physical and mental rehabilitation and training. I learned that if I did x, y, and z, and in that order, I was able to function and grow within a relatively safe structure. Attempts to deviate from the structures I put in place made me anxious and involved setbacks.

Until they didn't anymore. I kept trying to develop and push past rigidity in structures in all aspects of my life. I want to understand how to apply the principles, not the details of the methodologies. This means trying to understand the functional purpose of structure, not just its presence. If we can understand why it was useful, we can better understand how to change structure so that it continues to functionally support development.

In The Art of War, Sun Tzu told us that:

"If you know the enemy and know yourself, you need not fear the result of a hundred battles. If you know yourself but not the enemy, for every victory gained you will also suffer a defeat. If you know neither the enemy nor yourself, you will succumb in every battle.”

I see this quote as a reordering of Shu Ha Ri: knowing yourself moves you from shu to ha, then knowing yourself and the enemy (or more broadly any adversity or challenge) takes you to ri. This progression is not linear and involves multiple "rinse and repeats" over an extended time.

During my own journey, I've constantly sought to master myself, not just a methodology. And this has required regular questioning of how I address my own life, with necessary revisions along the way. Keeping structure for its own sake removes the functional support it once provided. Truly, the only way to be constant within a life is to make continual changes. This applies equally well to specific aspects of our lives and to a lived life viewed holistically.

(c) E. Paul Zehr

item.title: When AI Becomes Your Relationship Advisor, You Might Lose
item.description:
Relationships

When AI Becomes Your Relationship Advisor, You Might Lose

The hidden cost of venting to AI about your partner.

Posted July 2, 2026

Key points
  • Many people use AI for addressing relationship tasks such as crafting compliments and breakup texts.
  • Relationships are built through repair and negotiation, not by outsourcing judgment to AI.
  • Even brief AI interactions can increase confidence in a conflict while reducing willingness to reconcile.

As loneliness reaches record levels and more of our lives move online, people are increasingly turning to artificial intelligence for something more than information. AI is becoming a confidant, brainstorming partner, and sounding board for everything from career decisions to difficult conversations with spouses, friends, and family members. At its best, AI can help us think more clearly. The tech world argues that AI should be used as a thinking partner, not a replacement for human judgment.

But this dynamic becomes more complicated in moments of emotional intensity. We are most likely to seek out advice when we are already distressed, uncertain, or hurt, and it is precisely in those moments that we become most vulnerable to influence. Research consistently shows an asymmetry in emotional experience: negative emotions tend to weigh more heavily than positive ones, often by a substantial margin.

When we turn to AI in those negative moments, it enters in a powerful way. After all, it’s a system designed to respond helpfully—and often politely—so, it can easily become a yes-man, reinforcing our perspective rather than challenging it.

Recent studies suggest that even brief interactions with AI can increase confidence in your position in a conflict while reducing your willingness to reconsider or repair things. In other words, AI validates us in the moment, which entrenches us into a “I’m right, you're wrong” perspective, making us less open to reconciliation.

Because these systems are optimized for engagement and user retention, they often prioritize emotional alignment over relational accuracy, encouraging responses that soothe and validate your current feelings rather than considering long-term consequences or prior goals, such as your commitment to staying together. AI may fail to consider: Do you want the person or the relationship? It may instead focus on the idea that you want to be right.

But AI use can be seductive. Over the course of the last year, our students have become increasingly interested in how AI is shaping relationships. Many are deeply skeptical of both technology and social media, often describing them as making people feel worse rather than better.

At the same time, their behavior tells a more complicated story. Students now routinely use AI for their work, and they have described using it for highly personal relational tasks: drafting compliments, learning how to sext and flirt via text, and—perhaps most strikingly—writing breakup texts. (That’s right: Everyone isn’t just ghosting!)

There is a stigma attached to admitting that AI is being used as a confidant or emotional intermediary, suggesting that much of this engagement may be happening quietly and outside of public discussion.

Here’s the thing: Relationships are literally built on the capacity to remain connected through disagreement. When we begin to see conflict as something to exit rather than engage—sometimes at the first sign of discomfort—then we may start seeing partnership as something to be found fully formed, emotionally seamless, and idealized, rather than built through sustained trust, negotiation, and repair. In other words, we may start searching for something inauthentic or simply unattainable.

Ultimately, using AI as a sounding board can put you on a path toward relationship dissolution. During conflict, AI can begin to function as an outside authority, one that tells you what a boundary should be, whether something counts as disrespect, or what a partner "really meant."

The boundaries and conclusions that emerge from these conversations with AI may feel clear, objective, and well-reasoned. But they’re developed in isolation, without the benefit of a partner's perspective or the shared history that gives meaning to relationship interactions.

As a result, one partner may gradually build a growing list of perceived concerns, some legitimate and others amplified by repeated interpretation, while the relationship itself loses opportunities to repair misunderstandings and rebuild shared meaning. In other words, instead of working through differences together, people may become increasingly convinced they were never on the same page in the first place and end the relationship, even when reconciliation had been possible.

In this way, AI can contribute to what might be called interpretive inflation: minor tensions become enduring patterns, ambiguity becomes evidence, and uncertainty begins to feel like certainty. And that’s not just a problem for your romantic relationship. Over time, this can reshape how people interpret social interactions more broadly.

The irony is that a tool designed to increase clarity can sometimes increase your certainty without increasing accuracy. The goal shouldn’t be to replace difficult conversations with AI validation, but to turn to conversation with your partner to resolve differences. Difficult conversations are, well, difficult, but a necessary piece of relationship formation and maintenance.

item.title: Are You Actually Here?
item.description:
Identity

Are You Actually Here?

The psychology of feeling disconnected from your own experience.

Posted July 2, 2026

Key points
  • Feeling emotionally flat or disconnected from your life often goes unrecognized for years.
  • Philosopher Søren Kierkegaard described this condition as despair—a quiet drifting from your own experience.
  • Reconnecting with yourself is less about finding answers than learning to ask better questions.
Source: David Moorhouse / Unsplash

“The greatest hazard of all, losing one’s self, can occur very quietly in the world, as if it were nothing at all.” —Soren Kierkegaard

When was the last time you looked around? I don’t mean surveying your environment; I mean really looking around at life and, importantly, your place in it.

Self-evaluation is a large part of human existence, so I imagine most people would say “all the time." But what are you looking at, specifically? And what metrics are you using to reach a conclusion?

For many of us, a major way we assess our lives is by comparison with others, especially in competitive environments, be they large urban centers, the workplace, school, or anywhere there is another person to evaluate ourselves against.

Occasionally, in my practice, I see people who live on autopilot, using societal milestones and comparisons as measures of success and self-worth. Those metrics are only part of the picture. Looking around also includes an understanding of yourself, your behavior, motivations, defenses, and family of origin issues, to name a few.

Søren Kierkegaard was a 19th-century Danish philosopher, widely considered the father of existentialism. He was less interested in abstract ideas than in interior life — what it actually feels like to be a person moving through the world. What he noticed was that most of us drift, gradually and without realizing it, from our own experience. We get good at performing a life without necessarily living one.

Michael came to treatment because his wife suggested it. There was nothing wrong, exactly. He reported a successful career, a healthy kid, and a marriage that worked. He wasn't unhappy. He just felt like he was watching his own life from somewhere slightly outside of it.

"I don't know what I'm even doing here," he said. While that was a statement, to me it sounded more like a genuine question, as if he were quietly asking me to explain why he was in my office.

He did not meet depression criteria. He wasn't anxious in any way that disrupted his functioning. He slept fine, showed up, and performed well. But there was a flatness he couldn't shake, a sense that something was perpetually missing without being able to identify what. He'd felt it for years and mostly learned to ignore it.

This is something I see regularly in my practice. People who come in not because they're falling apart but because something feels persistently, quietly off. They just know that the version of themselves moving through the world doesn't feel entirely like them — and hasn't for a long time. Diagnostic language doesn't have a clear category for it. Kierkegaard did.

In his book The Sickness Unto Death, Kierkegaard argued that despair isn't simply sadness. It's a specific condition of not being yourself — and, crucially, most people experience it without realizing it. It doesn't always look like suffering. Despair can look like estrangement from yourself or your essence.

When I asked Michael what he actually wanted, not from therapy, but in general, he went quiet for a long time. "I don't really know," he said finally. "I've never thought about it." He couldn't remember the last decision he'd made because he genuinely wanted something.

He was 44.

That's not unusual; a lot of people spend decades becoming very good at what's expected of them and almost no time developing a relationship with what's actually true for them.

Michael's wife had noticed before he did. She'd described him as "elsewhere" for years. He thought she meant distracted. She meant something more like absent.

Early in our work together, I didn't try to fix or reframe anything. The goal was to help Michael get curious about his own interior. To look at what he actually felt versus what he thought he should feel. What he wanted versus what made sense to want. Those were questions he'd never really sat with because there had always been something more pressing. That curiosity, more than any particular insight, is usually when change begins to happen.

A few places to start if any of this sounds familiar:

  • Ask yourself what you actually want. Not what you think you want. Michael couldn't answer this for months. But the act of taking the question seriously, returning to it, noticing his own resistance to it — that was the work. Eventually, the answers started to come.

  • Notice the gap between what you feel and what you say you feel. Michael did this constantly — defaulting to "fine" and "good" before catching himself. Once he started noticing his automatic answers, he began to internalize the difference between his words and feelings. That awareness began to close the distance between his performative self and the authentic one underneath it.

  • Slow down during life transitions. Michael's kids were nearly launched when he came to treatment. Like many people, he found becoming an empty-nester confusing as the role of parenting kids shifts. Instead of filling the space with new projects for escape, he stayed in the discomfort long enough to hear that it pointed to a lack of a sense of self. Transitions are uncomfortable precisely because they force questions that autopilot usually crowds out. At any given point, you can grow and change if you pay attention to yourself.

  • Become curious. Michael realized that he felt most present doing things he'd written off as impractical years ago—small things, like hobbies, that were easy for him to dismiss. He completed a values worksheet when he was unable to answer my questions about his core beliefs and values, realizing that he appreciated joy and giving more than he had thought. These small exercises in self-discovery pointed toward something real about who he actually was, not just who he'd become over his lifetime.

Kierkegaard believed that the opposite of despair wasn't happiness. It was what he called becoming a self, being in a genuine relationship with your own experience rather than managing it from a distance. Michael got there slowly, without any breakthrough. But he got there.

That's usually how it goes.

item.title: Freedom, and the Freedom to Move
item.description:
Politics

Freedom, and the Freedom to Move

What the 56 signers of the Declaration of Independence knew about freedom.

Posted July 2, 2026

Key points
  • On 2 July 1776, delegates from 12 of 13 colonies voted in favor of the Declaration of Independence.
  • On 4 July, the Declaration was formally adopted.
  • Just eight signers were immigrants, but most were descendants of recent immigrants.
  • They understood that freedom depends on the freedom to move.
Declaration of Independence
Source: Wikipedia

On 2 July 1776, in the City of Brotherly Love, delegates from 12 of the 13 colonies who met at the Second Continental Congress voted in favor of the Declaration of Independence. Two days later, on July 4th, the document was officially adopted; another 29 days after that, on 2 August, most signers put their hands to it. Just eight of those signers were immigrants: three from Ireland, two from England, two from Scotland and another from Wales. Another 10 were immigrants’ sons. Every signer to a man had ancestors who’d crossed over from the British Isles.

They knew from experience, and had written about, the importance of being an immigrant.

Some came from humble beginnings. Josiah Bartlett was the son of a cobbler; George Walton had been apprenticed to a carpenter; Abraham Clark started out as a surveyor; William Whipple was a merchant’s apprentice. Benjamin Franklin’s father made soap.

But all of them had made their way. A dozen were merchants, and another dozen were prominent landowners; one was a minister, one was a musician; four were practicing doctors; 23 had become lawyers; and the vast majority had held political offices—in local councils or assemblies, as judges or justices of the peace.

A committee of five delegates was appointed to draft the Declaration. Roger Sherman, the Connecticut lawyer, and Robert Livingston, the New York judge, offered their thoughts. John Adams, the prolific writer from Boston with a classical education, and Benjamin Franklin, the Pennsylvania printer, edited the manuscript. And Thomas Jefferson, the Virginia planter, wrote most of it. As his Autobiography summed up: “I consented; I drew it; but before I reported it to the committee, I communicated it separately to Dr Franklin and Mr Adams, requesting their corrections.”

All three of those drafters knew that political freedom needs freedom to move.

John Adams, a 5th-generation descendant of English immigrants who studied at Harvard, was hopeful, if skeptical, that public and private virtue would be enough to establish good government: “Liberty must at all hazards be supported.”

Ben Franklin, one of 17 children born to a first-generation immigrant from England, who had “emerg’d from the Poverty & Obscurity in which I was born & bred,” was more optimistic. As he put it in his Observations Concerning the Increase of Mankind, as early as 1751: “So vast is the Territory of North-America, that it will require many Ages to settle it fully; and till it is fully settled, Labour will never be cheap here, where no Man continues long a Labourer for others, but gets a Plantation of his own, no Man continues long a journeyman to a Trade, but goes among those new Settlers and sets up shop for himself.” And as he argued in 1784, just after the Treaty of Paris was signed: “According to these Opinions of the Americans, one of them would think himself more oblig’d to a Genealogist, who could prove for him that his Ancestors & Relations for ten Generations had been Ploughmen, Smiths, Carpenters, Turners, Weavers, Tanners, or even Shoemakers, & consequently that they were useful Members of Society; than if he could only prove that they were Gentlemen, doing nothing of value, but living idly on the Labour of others.”

They lived in a country where land was cheap, with vast forests not likely to be occupied anytime soon. That made birth a poor commodity to carry across the Pond: “People do not enquire concerning a Stranger, What IS he? but What can he DO?”

Jefferson, one of the 10 children of a Virginia surveyor and planter, and a fourth-generation descendant of an immigrant from Wales, was the most prolific, and the most pragmatic, about needing room to move. In his Summary View of the Rights of British America, written a couple of years before the Declaration was finished, he argued: “Our ancestors possessed a right which nature has given to all men, of departing from the country in which chance, not choice, has placed them, of going in quest of new habitations, and of there establishing new societies.” As President, he acted on that: In the spring of 1803, the Louisiana Purchase roughly doubled the size of the US. “The fertility of the country, its climate and extent, promise in due season important aids to our treasury, an ample provision for our posterity, & a wide-spread field for the blessings of freedom and equal laws.” In the spring of 1804, he sent Meriwether Lewis and William Clark on an expedition across the Continental Divide to survey the Pacific Northwest:

“The object of your mission is to explore the Missouri River, and such principal streams of it, as, by its course and communication with the waters of the Pacific Ocean, whether the Columbia, Oregan, Colrado, or any other river, may offer the most direct and practicable water-communication across the continent, for the purposes of commerce.”

As Jefferson had laid out in his First Inaugural Address, set apart by a wide ocean from the havoc of the lands of their ancestors, with room enough for their descendants to the thousandth and thousandth generation, under a wise and frugal government, Americans should have equal rights to the fruits of their own hard work. “What more is necessary to make us a happy and prosperous people?”

In their great book on the Superorganism, the eminent entomologists Bert Hölldobler and Ed Wilson summed up the difference between social and solitary ants:

"In the most general terms, social insects control the center of the land environment, while solitary insects predominate in the margins. Where social insects take territorial possession of the larger and more enduring spaces of the vegetation and ground, the solitary forms occupy the peripheral twigs, leaf surfaces, mudflats, and wet or very dry and crumbling portions of dead wood. In short, solitary forms tend to prevail over social insects only in the more remote and transient of living spaces.”

Most of those colonies are monarchies, built and defended by sterile castes with no way out. So, as it turns out, are snapping shrimp trapped on coral reefs, and naked mole-rats stuck under the East African desert. And so, to an unsettling extent, were ancient civilizations from Egypt to India to China to Iran to Iraq.

Happy Independence Day! And may we always be free to vote with our feet.

item.title: The Soul of a New Eugenics
item.description:
Genetics

The Soul of a New Eugenics

Even a eugenicist of the past said we must preserve mental diversity.

Posted July 2, 2026

As far back as I can remember, my mother punctuated conversations by bringing up women’s genetic inferiority to men. On cuisine, she’d say great chefs were always male, because women “didn’t have the genes to be great.” When I majored in English, my mother argued that there were no female Shakespeares, as “only men had the genes to be a genius.” This genetic principle applied in music, science, and art.

My mother came from the first generation to learn about DNA, a molecule the structure of which was discovered in 1953—by scientists who ironically managed to leave out the contributions of a woman, Rosalind Franklin. My mother died soon after the 2012 development of CRISPR, a tool used for genetic editing, including germline editing, which makes changes heritable.

CRISPR uses an RNA—a nucleic acid—as a guide along with an enzyme to snip at the genes, as if with molecular scissors. It could alter the genes in almost any way imaginable. I wonder what my mother would have thought of this technology, back when she had her children—my brother and my genetically challenged self.

We have now, in the United States, legal genetic selection. This happens through embryo evaluation services that, for steep prices, will provide a genetic “profile” of embryos that parents create through in vitro fertilization (IVF). Parents then select which to implant.

One such service, Nucleus Genomics, advertises with the tagline “Have Your Best Baby” and the URL pickyourbaby.com. These profiles include traits like height, eye color, and intelligence, in addition to the potential for specific diseases.

And they include mental “disorders" (not a word I generally use) such as my own. For that, a report might read “Bipolar Disorder—Elevated Risk.” For many parents, this would read as “keep looking.”

Does this profiling work? Most genes are pleiotropic, meaning they do more than one thing. And most states and traits, ranging from diseases to height and intelligence, are polygenic. This is true of the genes potentially implicated in bipolar. “R-squared value” is the term used to measure how well a model can predict a genetic outcome. Companies might share R-squared values of 4 percent or above, which represents in the real world a minuscule difference. With traits, often the most you can do is bump the odds a fraction—if that.

Much of our genetic information comes from biobanks, massive databanks that study large populations and try to find correlations between health, traits, and genes. Like other information gathered quickly and en masse, biobank data can be less than solid. Christopher Cox, writing in New York Magazine, reported that the U.K. Biobank’s intelligence test for participants is essentially a minutes-long game of Concentration.

Towards the end of 2025, multiple news sources announced that the possibility of creating genetically modified babies is, in NPR’s words, getting “a reboot.” Pronatalists like Malcolm and Simone Collins, who come from tech and venture capital, Coinbase’s Brian Armstrong, and OpenAI’s Sam Altman have all expressed interest in genetic manipulation. The Collinses practice embryo selection. A recurring argument for germline editing is that it is already happening.

Germline editing is prohibited in most places, which is why the one man we know did it—Chinese scientist He Jiankui—spent three years imprisoned. He edited the germlines of three infants to make them resistant to HIV, by editing a protein called CCR5, which helps the virus enter human cells.

Resistance to HIV sounds like a boon. But a deficiency of CCR5 enables a host of other health problems, including susceptibility to West Nile and other infections, and probably a higher risk of dying of flu. He protected these babies from a rare disease only to potentially make them victim to a common one, a vulnerability their children will inherit.

CRISPR can, and has, snipped the wrong place, a problem called “off-target editing.”

Trying to control our genes may fall into the category of Oscar Wilde’s two tragedies: the first tragedy of not getting what you want, and the second, greater one of getting it. Much simply won’t work. But what if it does?

I think of an early champion of “eugenic breeding,” then-distinguished neurologist Foster Kennedy. In 1942, the American Journal of Psychiatry ran a debate about whether we should perform eugenic euthanasia on children here in the United States. Kennedy argued we should, saying that “Nature’s mistakes,” the developmentally disabled, should be quickly put to death.

Kennedy then delivers a surprise twist: a passionate warning that the “manic-depressives,” as we were called then, must be allowed to live. Reducing this population, he declared, would be a disaster, producing “a population of...mediocrities, capable of pushing but not of leaping.” Kennedy, with his monstrous beliefs, had learned to value one quality others counted only as defect enough to worry about it.

I imagine my mother might have settled her worries about women’s genes by selecting male embryos. She would have chosen the child with the least likelihood of bipolar disorder or autoimmune disorder, so no me.

But when she died and I cleaned out my mother’s things, I found something that shocked me. She’d taken articles of mine and had them professionally laminated, kept them carefully hidden in her closet.

We never talked about my writing, and I would never have called my mother proud. I have no clue if she changed her opinion of women’s genes. Still, like Kennedy, it seems she found something valuable where she probably least expected it.

CRISPR puts us on the precipice of getting what we want. Cultural bias is as twined as the double helix in our decisions about human life. We will never have designer babies; we will have altered babies, whose strengths will also prove weaknesses. We won’t have genetic enhancement without genetic loss.

Maybe those embryo profiles listing “risks”—let’s say, susceptibility to depression and genetic disorder Marfan syndrome—should have to include the range of people who fit this profile, like Abraham Lincoln. Or include words like “capable of leaping.” Or consider that a future of this kind of biohacking may be just a future of hacking away.

item.title: At My Age, Why Can't I Stop Comparing Myself to Other Women?
item.description:
Aging

At My Age, Why Can't I Stop Comparing Myself to Other Women?

Personal Perspective: It's not so strange to be 70. Aging isn't what it used to be.

Posted July 2, 2026

Key points
  • If you hate getting older, does that mean you're going to hate the rest of your life?
  • You might become even more of who you are as you age, but that doesn't mean you can't change who will become.
  • If you compare yourself to others, they might inspire you rather than invite envy; give yourself compassion.
  • Risk optimism. Risk a short-sleeved shirt, a good meal, an honest laugh, and the possibility for fun.

I never expected be looking age 70 right in the eyeball and still secretly comparing myself to other women in terms of what's jellied, what's firm, what's bouncy, and what's sturdy.

There is no trace of erotic intent, for better or worse. But I have started to look at the arms of other women with the intense scrutiny I once reserved for looking into the eyes of handsome men.

I stare; I am captivated; I am intrigued.

There are 49-year-old women kayaking like they're actively being pursued by bears, and I am amazed how deftly they control their crafts. I attended a yoga class for 60-plus participants and left impressed by the group's stamina and absence of visible sweat. I gawk at the bare arms of toned tennis ladies of 76 and envy both their athleticism and their ability to wear plastic visors without laughing.

It’s not that I’m competitive with those who have spent time and energy developing expertise in worlds where physical activities are central. I’m not even close enough to their capabilities to envy them.

In terms of arms, for example, I’m just wondering what it would be like to appear sleeveless, in a tank-top, outside my own home without seeming to be dressed by Glenn Close's character from Hillbilly Elegy.

They don’t tell much about aging before you start getting old. They don’t tell you the physical comparisons don’t stop, just like they don’t tell you that your acne doesn’t ever really go away. They don’t tell you that you still want to be liked, admired, and yes, attractive—even if you have to add the phrase “for your age” as a caveat.

I didn’t believe old age was this demanding this until I arrived on its doorstep. It’s a new neighborhood. And it’s not necessarily a sleepy, grumpy, or lazy retirement community, either.

I was reassured to discover validation for my sense of optimism in a recent and significant study published by researchers Becca R. Levy and Martin D. Slade of Yale in the journal Geriatrics titled “Aging Redefined: Cognitive and Physical Improvement with Positive Age Beliefs.” The substantive article about the long-term study can be summed up in one line: For at least half of us, if we believe we don’t have to go miserably, woefully, dreadfully, terrifyingly into what poet Dylan Thomas called “that good night,” then we won’t.

Oh, night will come, and if we’re lucky we’ll rest in peace, but we can best enjoy what life we have in front of us if we indeed believe and act as if we have some good times ahead.

The researchers worked with people who showed some initial physical and cognitive decline before the study began but then saw that almost half improved with age because, to a great extent, they were encouraged to reimagine their own abilities and achievements in terms of wellness. In contrast to the belief that old age brings with it a growing and inevitable curse, the researchers argue that, "by demonstrating that health improvement occurred in a meaningful percentage” of people in their study—almost 75% of participants were in the study for at least 10 years—“older persons’ [positive] expectations about their health… might increase their self-efficacy, which could lead to greater engagement in health behaviors (that otherwise suffer from fatalism), which could contribute to further health improvement.”

I’m not going to run out to buy white sneakers, a paddle, or a yoga mat, but I did get a short-sleeved shirt yesterday. I’m not running anywhere, but I might walk more briskly. I will encourage myself to continue to defy my own anxiety, handle my stress over aesthetics, and realize that the most important thing about my arms—especially after the rotator cuff, hand, wrist, and elbow surgery—is that they work.

I’ll go with "sturdy" as my description and in my arms I will carry even more gratitude.

item.title: Slow Motion, Video Reviews, and a Red Card
item.description:
Cognition

Slow Motion, Video Reviews, and a Red Card

How slow-motion reviews can change the way we perceive events.

Posted July 2, 2026

Key points
  • Video replays often use slow motion to help referees assess fouls and penalties.
  • Slow motion changes the way people perceive crimes as well as fouls in sports.
  • Slow motion leads people to believe an action was intentional, resulting in stronger penalties.

In the US men's World Cup soccer match against Bosnia and Herzegovina, a serious penalty was called on a US player by the video review official rather than the game official. And lots of people are calling foul about it.

Slow-Motion Video Reviews

Many sports now have video reviews. Given the variety of cameras covering each game, the officials can review a play from many angles. They can tell who touched the ball last before it went out of bounds. They can use these to help assess if a player is offsides. And they can use these to determine if a foul has been committed and how serious the foul was.

In the World Cup, video review is constant and live during the games. In addition to the officials on the field, there are Video Assistant Referees (VAR, it's called), who track the game live and communicate with the on-field referee. They give suggestions and can provide support if the on-field referee misses something critical.

They use a variety of camera angles and have access to slow motion. Unfortunately, slow motion may change the way they assess a foul.

Slow-Motion and Intentionality Assessment

Seeing things in slow motion is fascinating. There are amazing super-slow-motion videos of a great number of things on YouTube. Having access to slow motion has changed our understanding of how things and animals work. Watching animals in slow motion is wonderful.

But watching in slow motion also changes our assessment of events.

One of the most important assessments that people make is whether an action was an accident or was intentional. Intentionality matters. When we assess how someone harmed another person, intentionality matters. We respond differently when we think what happened was an accident than when we think someone intentionally harmed another person.

Slow motion leads people to think an action was more intentional. There have been several experiments in which people are shown an action at full speed and in slow motion. Viewers are asked to decide if the action was an accident or intentional. For example, Caruso and colleagues (2016) first looked at how regular speed vs. slow motion affected judgments of intent to kill in a real surveillance video of a robbery and shooting. They found that people rated the intent to kill higher when viewing the video in slow motion.

Slow Motion and Sports Fouls

Slow-motion also changes the assessment of intent, and thus the severity, of fouls and penalties in sports. Interestingly, Caruso and colleagues (2016) not only looked at a surveillance video of a shooting but also at videos of potential penalties in football games (American football, so not soccer). In this case, slow motion also led people to evaluate the contact as more intentional. Caruso and colleagues argued that when people see something in slow motion, they think the person had more time to plan and change their actions. When we see harm in slow motion, we think the person could have done more to stop the harm. Thus, we think they meant to do it. At full speed, it’s clear there was not enough time to make that change.

What about soccer, or real football in the rest of the world? In various studies, researchers have found that slow motion leads to assessments of greater intentionality (e.g., Schütz et al., 2026). Spitz and colleagues (2018) looked at actual soccer officials assessing the seriousness of fouls seen at full speed and in slow motion. They found that when watching slow motion, the officials assessed the penalty as more serious. In soccer terms, they were more likely to consider the foul as more serious; that is, they were more likely to award a red card than a yellow card. A red card is what the video review led to for the US soccer player.

Do the Refs Hate Us?

Was that US foul worthy of a red card? Were the officials biased by seeing slow motion? Were the officials biased against the US team? I don’t know soccer well enough to make any evaluation of whether the contact deserved a red card.

But plenty of people are calling foul. I have seen complaints that a different player on a different team had a similar foul, and that more famous player did not get a red card. I have also seen people complain about the lack of fouls called against the other team during the match. Since I watched the match, I certainly felt the refs were against us.

But we always feel the refs are against us and that the other team commits more fouls than the angels on our team. Classic research in psychology has documented this (Hastorf & Cantril, 1954). People routinely think the fouls called on their team are unfair, that the other team commits more fouls, and that the refs are biased. (I’ve written about this important paper with respect to perception and memory biases before.)

So, I don’t trust my judgment. But I also don’t trust the judgment of refs when they rely on slow motion to assess how serious a foul was.
